item.research_question: Can a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy be developed that exhibits superior radiation resistance compared to pure tungsten, specifically avoiding the formation of irradiation-induced dislocation loops under fusion-relevant conditions?
item.material_system: Quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V high-entropy alloy with atomic composition 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V
item.processing_route: Magnetron sputtering deposition from pure metal targets (99.99% purity) at room temperature and 3 mtorr pressure; deposition powers of 192 W (Cr), 312 W (V), 277 W (Ta), and 300 W (W) with 20 W bias radio frequency power; film thicknesses of ~100 nm for TEM and ~3 μm for mechanical testing
item.test_conditions: In situ irradiation with 1-MeV Kr+2 ions at 1073 K (dpa rates 0.0006 and 0.0016 dpa s−1) up to 8 dpa; ex situ irradiation with 3-MeV Cu+ ions at 773 K and 1050 K up to a peak dose of ~17 dpa; thermal annealing up to 1073 K; nanoindentation and nanoDMA testing
key_findings: The as-deposited alloy exhibits a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of grains in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and ultrafine regions (100 to 500 nm).
A unique 4-nm lamella-like compositional layering structure was revealed by atom probe tomography (APT) in the as-deposited state.
No irradiation-created dislocation loops were observed even after 8 dpa of irradiation at 1073 K.
Black spots observed after thermal annealing and irradiation were identified as Cr- and V-rich second-phase precipitates (~3 to 5 nm in size) rather than dislocation loops.
The as-deposited samples showed a hardness of 14 GPa with near negligible irradiation hardening.
Modeling predicts the formation of Cr- and V-rich precipitates due to negative enthalpies of mixing for W-Ta, W-V, and Cr-V binaries.
Theoretical modeling suggests equal mobilities of vacancies and self-interstitials are the origin of the exceptional radiation tolerance.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that the exceptional radiation tolerance arises from the equal mobilities of point defects (vacancies and self-interstitials), which maximizes the recombination probability and minimizes defect clustering. This equal mobility is attributed to the rough energy landscape induced by local lattice distortion and chemical disparity in the high-entropy alloy. Additionally, the high density of grain boundaries acts as preferential recombination/annihilation sites for defects.
item.limitations: The study was conducted on thin films rather than bulk materials; the exact mechanism for the equal defect mobilities is not fully elucidated beyond the correlation with the energy landscape; the procedure to distinguish precipitates from dislocation loops using TEM breaks down for asymmetric strain fields or non-edge dislocation loops.
item.future_work: The authors state that the suitability of these alloys for bulk production coupled with their exceptional radiation resistance makes them ideal structural materials for applications requiring extreme irradiation conditions, implying a need for bulk synthesis and further testing.
quotes: No sign of irradiation-created dislocation loops, even after 8 dpa, was observed.

Theoretical modeling combining ab initio and Monte Carlo techniques predicts the formation of Cr- and V-rich second-phase particles and points at equal mobilities of point defects as the origin of the exceptional radiation tolerance.

The fact that no clustering is experimentally observed indicates that, in the HEA described in this work, this is a plausible case, i.e., the mobilities of vacancies and self-interstitials are similar as oppose to what happens in pure W.
